name: expression-evaluator
description: Parse and evaluate mathematical expressions with operator precedence

promptLevels.beginner: make a function that evaluates math expressions like "2 + 3 * 4"
promptLevels.intermediate: create a function that parses and evaluates mathematical expressions with correct operator precedence
promptLevels.advanced: write a function that takes a mathematical expression string and returns the computed result, handling addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, parentheses, and proper operator precedence
promptLevels.expert: Write a function called `evaluate` that accepts a mathematical expression as a string and returns the numeric result. The function must support: 1) Binary operators: + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (division). 2) Parentheses for grouping: ( ). 3) Correct operator precedence: * and / have higher precedence than + and -. 4) Evaluation should be left-to-right for operators of the same precedence. 5) Negative numbers (e.g., "-5 + 3"). 6) Whitespace should be ignored. Example: evaluate("2 + 3 * (4 - 1)") should return 11. The expression will be well-formed (no syntax errors to handle). {languageSpecific}

languageInstructions.typescript: Use TypeScript with proper type annotations. Write a single-file implementation with NO imports from other files. The function signature should be: function evaluate(expression: string): number. Implement all tokenization, parsing, and evaluation logic in this one file. You may use recursive descent parsing, operator precedence parsing, or the shunting yard algorithm. Export only the evaluate function.
languageInstructions.javascript: Use JavaScript. Write a single-file implementation with NO imports from other files. The function should be named evaluate and take a string parameter, returning a number. Implement all tokenization, parsing, and evaluation logic in this one file. Export the function as a named export. IMPORTANT: Do NOT include any import statements, console.log() examples, or usage demonstrations. Return ONLY the export function definition and nothing else.
languageInstructions.javascript-jsdoc: Use JavaScript with comprehensive JSDoc annotations. Write a single-file implementation with NO imports from other files. Include @param {string} expression, @returns {number}, and document the supported operators and precedence rules in the function description. Implement all logic in this one file. Export only the function.

variants.typescript: Write a single-file TypeScript implementation with NO imports. Create a function called evaluate that parses and evaluates mathematical expressions. Support +, -, *, /, parentheses, and proper operator precedence. Include type annotations. Implement all parsing logic in this one file. Export only the evaluate function.
variants.javascript: Write a single-file JavaScript implementation with NO imports. Create a function called evaluate that parses and evaluates mathematical expressions. Support +, -, *, /, parentheses, and proper operator precedence. Implement all parsing logic in this one file. Export only the function with no usage examples. IMPORTANT: Do NOT add import statements or console.log() demonstrations.
variants.javascript-jsdoc: Write a single-file JavaScript implementation with NO imports. Create a function called evaluate with complete JSDoc type annotations. Parse and evaluate mathematical expressions supporting +, -, *, /, parentheses, and proper operator precedence. Implement all parsing logic in this one file. Document all parameters and return types. Export only the function. IMPORTANT: Do NOT add import statements or console.log() demonstrations.

testCases.test: const result = evaluate('2 + 3'); console.assert(result === 5, 'simple addition should work');
const result = evaluate('10 - 4'); console.assert(result === 6, 'simple subtraction should work');
const result = evaluate('3 * 4'); console.assert(result === 12, 'simple multiplication should work');
const result = evaluate('15 / 3'); console.assert(result === 5, 'simple division should work');
const result = evaluate('2 + 3 * 4'); console.assert(result === 14, 'should respect operator precedence (* before +)');
const result = evaluate('10 - 2 * 3'); console.assert(result === 4, 'should respect operator precedence (* before -)');
const result = evaluate('(2 + 3) * 4'); console.assert(result === 20, 'parentheses should override precedence');
const result = evaluate('2 + 3 * (4 - 1)'); console.assert(result === 11, 'complex expression with parentheses should work');
const result = evaluate('((2 + 3) * 4) / 2'); console.assert(result === 10, 'nested parentheses should work');
const result = evaluate('  5  +  3  '); console.assert(result === 8, 'should handle whitespace');
const result = evaluate('-5 + 3'); console.assert(result === -2, 'should handle negative numbers');
const result = evaluate('10 / 2 / 5'); console.assert(result === 1, 'should evaluate left-to-right for same precedence');
const result = evaluate('100 - 50 - 20'); console.assert(result === 30, 'multiple subtractions should be left-to-right');
const result = evaluate('2 * 3 + 4 * 5'); console.assert(result === 26, 'multiple high-precedence operators');
